facts.statement: Prior to 2007, LIBOR was standardly used as the risk-free proxy for discounting. Because LIBOR is an unsecured bank borrowing rate carrying default and liquidity risk, the 2007-2008 crisis forced trading desks to adopt OIS discounting.
An Overnight Indexed Swap (OIS) exchanges a fixed interest rate for the geometric average of overnight central bank rates (Fed Funds in the US, SONIA in the UK, ESTR in Europe).

The LIBOR-OIS spread serves as a barometer of interbank credit and liquidity risk. In normal tranquil conditions it is 10 to 15 basis points; during the October 2008 Lehman collapse it spiked to 364 basis points.

Under standard ISDA Credit Support Annexes (CSAs), derivative cash flows must be discounted at the interest rate paid on posted cash collateral, which is strictly the overnight rate, making OIS discounting mathematically mandatory.

The Multi-Curve Framework decouples forward curve projections from discount curves: forward LIBOR/IBOR floating cash flows are projected using tenor-specific forward curves, but all cash flows are discounted back using the single continuous OIS zero curve.

Credit Valuation Adjustment: CVA = (1 - R) sum [ v(t_i) * EPE(t_i) * P(t_{i-1} < tau <= t_i) ], where R is recovery rate, v(t_i) is OIS discount factor, EPE is Expected Positive Exposure, and P is marginal default probability.
Holistic Total Derivative Valuation (XVA): Total Price = RiskFreeValue - CVA + DVA - FVA - MVA - KVA.

Following the LIBOR manipulation scandal and market illiquidity, global regulators mandated the transition to Nearly Risk-Free Rates (RFRs): SOFR for USD, SONIA for GBP, ESTR for EUR, and TONOR for JPY, utilizing ISDA fallback spreads.
